a.raw: you cant send me back i need a home she wept
a.why: Opening quotation mark and a capital to start the speech, an apostrophe in can’t, a capital on I, an exclamation point for the strong feeling, a comma inside the closing quotation mark, and a period after wept.

b.raw: please dont send me away im trying to be good anne sobbed
b.why: The same two-part pattern: quotation marks around everything she says, apostrophes in don’t and I’m, a capital I, an exclamation point after the first part, a comma inside the closing quotation mark, and a capital on Anne because it is a name.

scholar.journal-q1: … and explain why Marilla’s plan makes sense to her, even if it sounds unkind.
scholar.journal-q2: … then say whether Montgomery tells you Anne’s feeling or shows it, and how you can tell.
scholar.journal-q3: … and compare it with how Anne felt the night before: what changed, and what did not?

fill1.h1: Before a b, this prefix ends in the letter you close your lips to say.
fill1.why: com- means “with” or “together.” Before b and p it is spelled with an m, so comfortable.

fill2.h1: Before an f, the prefix that means “with” is spelled with an n.
fill2.why: con- means “with.” To confess is to tell the truth to someone else, owning up to them.

fill3.h1: Say the whole word out loud. Before a t, which spelling do you hear, m or n?
fill3.why: con- comes before t, the way it does in contain and continue. Someone content is satisfied with what they have.

fill4.h1: You met this word in the vocabulary match. Before a p, the prefix ends in m.
fill4.why: com- + panion: a companion is the one who goes along with you.

vfill1.h1: The word goes before “old mare,” so it describes the horse. Which bank word means calm and peaceful?
vfill1.why: A placid horse is calm and steady — nothing startles it, not even a talkative girl.

vfill2.h1: Anne makes a picture in her mind. Which bank word is something you do inside your head?
vfill2.why: To imagine is to picture something that is not in front of you.

vfill3.h1: The girl sat beside Matthew the whole ride. Which word names someone who goes with you?
vfill3.why: A companion is someone you spend time with — and Matthew had a talkative one.

g4w7ff1.h1: Knife does not just add an s. Listen to the f when there is more than one.
g4w7ff1.why: The f changes to v before -es: knives. Same with leaf and leaves, wife and wives.

g4w7ff2.h1: One child, two… This plural does not end in s at all.
g4w7ff2.why: children uses an old ending, -ren, instead of -s.

g4w7ff3.h1: One goose, a whole flock of… The change happens in the middle of the word.
g4w7ff3.why: oo turns to ee: geese, just like foot and feet, tooth and teeth.

g4w7ff4.h1: Say it: one woman, two… Only one letter changes.
g4w7ff4.why: The a becomes e: women, just like man and men.

s4w7ff1.h1: Story ends in a consonant and then y. What happens to that y?
s4w7ff1.why: Consonant + y: change the y to i and add -es. stories.

s4w7ff2.h1: Try saying “boxs.” Your mouth needs one more sound.
s4w7ff2.why: Words ending in x, s, sh, ch or z add -es: boxes.

s4w7ff3.h1: Window ends in w. Does it need anything more than the ordinary ending?

s4w7ff4.h1: Look at the letter just before the y in daisy.
s4w7ff4.why: s is a consonant, so the y changes to i and you add -es: daisies.

copia.seed: Marilla came briskly forward as Matthew opened the door.
eg: When she heard the buggy in the yard, Marilla came briskly forward as Matthew opened the door.
Marilla hurried briskly forward as Matthew opened the door.
Marilla came briskly forward into the lamplight as Matthew opened the kitchen door.

connector: Yesterday Anne talked the whole eight miles from the station, and Matthew barely said a word. Today the buggy pulls into the yard and Marilla comes to the door. Two chapters: one evening that goes badly, and the morning after it. As you read, keep asking today’s question. Does Montgomery tell you how Anne feels, or does she let you watch?

transcripts.welcome: Here is today's question, and it is a hard one. When somebody gets bad news, how does a writer show us how they feel — by telling us outright, or by letting us watch what they say and do? By the end of today you will be able to use the details on the page to explain how Anne takes the worst news of her life. Watch closely. It happens quickly.
transcripts.guide1: Three chapters, three surprises. Mrs Rachel, then Matthew, and today Marilla. Montgomery is showing you one arrival through three different pairs of eyes, and asking you to notice that they don't agree. Keep that with you. First the word work — it's the same pattern you've been building all week, and today it should start to feel easy.
transcripts.guide2: Two chapters today, and they pull in opposite directions. The first is an evening when Anne hears news she cannot imagine her way out of. The second is a morning at a window. Watch what her imagination does in each one. Does it rescue her, or can it not reach that far? The house stays exactly the same between the two chapters. Only Anne changes.
transcripts.guide3: You've just watched Anne go from the worst evening of her life to a morning at a window, with the same house around her both times. That is the whole idea of perspective, in two chapters. Carry it into your answers. And carry it into your own story, where your character is starting to sound like somebody.
transcripts.wgrd: Writers hide opinions inside single words. When a dress is called ugly, or a face is called eager, somebody is doing the judging. Today two grown-ups look at the same girl, and they do not choose the same words for her. As you read, catch one word that belongs to Marilla and one that belongs to Matthew, and ask whose eyes the narrator lent you.
transcripts.dol: This one is somebody talking again, but this time she says two things in a row, and each part needs its own ending. Watch where the strong feeling goes, and where the sentence takes a breath before the speaker. Two words have been squeezed short, and one little word is standing small where it should stand tall. The model shows you every piece.
transcripts.morphology: Today you build the words yourself. Here is the trick that decides it. Say the word out loud and feel your lips. If they press together for the next sound, the word part that means together ends with an m. If they don't, it ends with an n. Your mouth already knows the spelling. You just have to listen to it.
transcripts.vocabulary: Knowing what a word means is one thing. Putting it into a sentence where it fits is harder, and it is the test that really counts. Read each sentence all the way to the end before you choose. The words around the gap are clues, and one of them usually tells you exactly what kind of word belongs there.
transcripts.grammar: No word bank today, so every plural has to come from you. These are the words English refuses to make regular, and no rule will rescue you. You simply have to know them, the way you know your friends' names. Say each one out loud before you type it. If it sounds wrong with an ordinary ending, trust your ear.
transcripts.spelling: Today you build the plurals yourself, and each one hides a small decision. Look at the very last letter of the word before you add anything. Is it a letter that needs an extra beat to say? Is it a y with a consonant right in front of it? That last letter makes the decision for you, if you let it.
transcripts.read: Give yourself time today. There are two places to stop, one at the end of each chapter, and they ask very different things. The first is about someone who wants to keep Anne and can hardly say why. The second is about a view from a window. Stop both times, even when you want to keep reading. The stopping is where the thinking happens.
transcripts.chapter: Underneath these three questions is today's big one: does Montgomery tell you how Anne feels, or show you? When the second question asks for one sentence from Anne, choose one where she never names her feeling, but you know it anyway. That kind of sentence is your proof. It shows the feeling instead of telling it.
transcripts.wordconn: Your spelling answer is already saved, so here is the connection. All week, the last letter of a word has decided what happens to it. In these two chapters, one small fact decides what happens to Anne. She is a girl, not a boy. One detail at the end of a word, one detail about a person, and everything after it changes.
transcripts.workshop: Today's writing asks for the hardest feeling to show: disappointment. You just watched Anne take the worst news of her life, and Montgomery never once writes that she was sad. Borrow that. Let your character do something with their hands, or say one thing out loud, or go very quiet. Then stop, and let the reader feel it.
